'''Frank Henry Field''' (February 27, 1922 – April 12, 2013) was an American chemist and mass spectrometrist known for his work in the development of [[chemical ionization]].<ref name="Obituary">{{cite news |url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/nytimes/obituary.aspx?pid=164364120 |title= FRANK H. FIELD Obituary |work=New York Times |date=2013-04-21 |accessdate=2014-10-13 }}</ref><ref name="Chait2014">{{cite journal|last1=Chait|first1=Brian|title=Frank H. Field (1922–2013)|journal=Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry|volume=25|issue=5|year=2014|pages=702–704|issn=1044-0305|doi=10.1007/s13361-014-0866-3|pmid=24658810|bibcode=2014JASMS..25..702C|s2cid=11398163}}</ref><ref name="ASMS">{{cite web |url=http://www.asms.org/asms-news/2013/04/19/frank-h.-field-pioneer-in-mass-spectrometry-and-the-study-of-gaseous-ion-chemistry-dies-at-91 |title=Frank H. Field, Pioneer in Mass Spectrometry and the Study of Gaseous Ion Chemistry, Dies at 91 |accessdate=2014-10-13 }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Frank Field was born in [[Keansburg, New Jersey]], on February 27, 1922. His father died two months after he was born and his mother died in 1933, after which he was raised by his aunt in [[Cliffside Park, New Jersey]]. He attended [[Duke University]], where he studied chemistry, receiving his B.S. degree in chemistry in 1943, M.S. in 1944, and Ph.D. in 1948.<ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Frank H. Field |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/field-frank-h|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name="Transcript">{{cite book|first= Michael A. |last=Grayson|title=Frank H. Field, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by Michael A. Grayson at Durham, North Carolina on 9-10 December 2009 |date=10 December 2009 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/field_fh_0636_full.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref>

==Professional career==
Field took a position as an instructor at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] in 1947 and became an assistant professor in 1949. In 1952, he took a position as a research chemist at [[Humble Oil]] in [[Baytown, Texas]], where he, along with [[Burnaby Munson]], discovered chemical ionization.<ref name="Field1990">{{cite journal|last1=Field|first1=F. H.|title=The early days of chemical ionization: A reminiscence|journal=Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry|volume=1|issue=4|year=1990|pages=277–283|issn=1044-0305|doi=10.1016/1044-0305(90)85001-3|pmid=24248819|doi-access=free}}</ref>
In 1966, he moved to [[Esso]] Research and Development Company in [[Linden, New Jersey]], where he rose through the ranks to become a senior research associate. In 1970 he took a position as a professor at [[Rockefeller University]] and became emeritus in 1989.<ref name="OH"/><ref name="Transcript"/>

==Awards and honors==
Field was a [[Guggenheim Fellow]] in 1963–1964 and was president of the [[American Society for Mass Spectrometry]] from 1972 to 1974.<ref name="OH"/><ref name="Transcript"/> In 1987 he became a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name="AAAS">{{cite web|title=Frank Field|url=https://www.aaas.org/historic-fellow/field-frank-h|website=American Association for the Advancement of Science|accessdate=20 February 2018|archive-date=20 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180220213046/https://www.aaas.org/historic-fellow/field-frank-h|url-status=dead}}</ref> The Frank H. Field and [[Joe L. Franklin]] Award for Outstanding Achievement in Mass Spectrometry, given by the [[American Chemical Society]], was created in 1983. Field received the award in 1988.<ref>{{cite web|title=Frank H. Field and Joe L. Franklin Award for Outstanding Achievement in Mass Spectrometry|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/frank-h-field-and-joe-l-franklin-award-for-outstanding-achievement-in-mass-spectrometry.html|website=American Chemical Society|accessdate=20 February 2018}}</ref>
